segments.t: As Denis and Katya step into the apartment kitchen, Denis's roommate Senya and his wife Marina greet them. Senya immediately jokes about Denis's overnight guest until Marina invites the young couple to eat breakfast together. Let's listen to their cheerful breakfast conversation in Russian.
Now let's go through the breakfast conversation in the kitchen line by line.
'Hey there, who do we have here?' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'Hello, I was giving her tea.' Denis uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'Good morning to all of you.' Katya uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'Senya, why are you embarrassing people?' Notice how Russian puts 'people' and 'to people' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'All right, let's go have breakfast together.' Here Senya anchors the thought on 'let's go' and finishes on 'to have breakfast', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'Have you two been dating for a long time?' Russian uses the present tense with an adverb meaning long ago for an action that continues now.
'Well, there is a very long story there.' Denis pairs 'very, really' with 'history' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'We have been friends for a very long time.' The first-person plural present verb expresses an ongoing friendship that started in the past.
'And we are only dating starting today.' Here Denis anchors the thought on 'are dating' and finishes on 'today', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'Today will be our first day.' The future form of to be links the temporal adverb to an ordinal numeral and masculine noun.
'Yes, Katyusha, eat up, eat.' Denis centers this short reply on 'eat', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning.

'Thank you, everything is very tasty.' Katya uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away. Let's listen to the full kitchen dialogue again without interruption.

Denis proudly explains that he and Katya have been friends for a long time and are starting their first day as a couple. Listen for the reciprocal reflexive verbs meaning to be friends and to date. See you next time!
